summary:
Northern Ireland stands under the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 Supreme Court regime, which now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. Trans visitors in Northern Ireland therefore use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.

Prison placement follows the same rule across the United Kingdom. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, ruled the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory custody guidance unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; that guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in prisons matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. Challengers had argued that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. A visitor arrested anywhere in the United Kingdom should expect placement by sex at birth, with contested suicide-risk arguments surrounding that outcome.

Searching and strip-searching follow the same rule. British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, with trans women searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; the prior policy had permitted a trans woman staff member to conduct an intimate search of a woman holding a Gender Recognition Certificate. Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025 states that in custody and stop-and-search, any search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear is conducted on the basis of biological sex, though where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

The direction of travel is a court- and watchdog-led rollback rather than executive hostility, and it is contested at international level: on 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

Northern Ireland's devolved administration has moved in the same direction on documents of its own. On 8 September 2025 Education Minister Paul Givan requested removal of guidance supporting transgender pupils from the Education Authority website, and the guidance was withdrawn; he argued that it conflicted with departmental policy and with the law in Northern Ireland. The withdrawn guidance had recommended that trans pupils be allowed to use changing rooms matching their gender identity, and teachers' representatives warned that removal ignores the practical realities.

Protection machinery in Northern Ireland has been blocked at executive level. On 14 December 2025 it was reported that other executive parties had blocked Justice Minister Naomi Long's plan to add transgender people as a protected characteristic in Northern Ireland's new hate-crime legislation. Long had sought approval in early November with a response deadline in mid-November, and the bill had carried executive agreement since December 2024. She cited Police Service of Northern Ireland statistics of close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes.
tangentialFactors:
Northern Ireland's education and justice functions are devolved, so the two executive-level decisions recorded here concern bodies that do not set passport, entry, marriage or criminal law, all of which remain uniform across the United Kingdom.

The hate-crime bill had executive agreement from December 2024 before the transgender provision was blocked, which indicates that the obstacle was the addition of the characteristic rather than the legislation as a whole.

Teachers' representatives publicly contested the withdrawal of the transgender-pupils guidance, arguing that it ignores the practical realities, so the education position is disputed within Northern Ireland rather than settled.

The single-sex-services rollback described in the national framework is driven by courts and an equality watchdog, whereas the two Northern Ireland decisions were taken by ministers and executive parties; the outcomes point the same way through different machinery.
localsOnly:
Pupils in Northern Ireland schools no longer have Education Authority guidance recommending that trans pupils use changing rooms matching their gender identity, following the withdrawal requested by Education Minister Paul Givan in September 2025.

Transgender people are not a protected characteristic in Northern Ireland's new hate-crime legislation as blocked in December 2025, so a resident reporting a motivated offence cannot rely on that status in sentencing provisions, while Justice Minister Naomi Long cited close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes recorded by the Police Service of Northern Ireland.

Residents in custody or subject to stop-and-search in the United Kingdom are searched on the basis of biological sex where removal beyond outer clothing is involved, with an officer of a person's lived gender to be provided on request where that differs.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the transgender provision in Northern Ireland's hate-crime legislation was later reinstated, amended or dropped is unresolved in the sources available for this entry; the latest sourced position is the block reported on 14 December 2025.

Whether replacement guidance for transgender pupils was issued after the September 2025 withdrawal, and what day-to-day practice Northern Ireland schools now follow on changing facilities, is not sourced here.

Enforcement of the August 2026 single-sex-spaces code by Northern Ireland bodies specifically is not sourced; the code is described as nationwide, but no Northern Ireland compliance example appears in the inventory.

Claims about paramilitary-pattern violence against LGB&T people in Northern Ireland appear in earlier framing of this jurisdiction but are not carried in the current source inventory, and are therefore not asserted here.
